summary.text: At \(n=140\), comparison of \(5n^2\) with \(4z^2\) and \(4(z+1)^2\) gives the needed floors \(180,175,160,156\), hence \(a(161)=542\), \(a(157)=528\), \(a(144)=484\), and \(a(140)=471\). The proposed recurrence would therefore require \(542=528+484-471=541\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=2n+\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\frac n4\right\rfloor
\qquad(n\ge 1).
\]
We disprove the proposed recurrence by exhibiting a failure at \(n=140\).

First, we record how the irrational floor terms will be evaluated without using decimal approximations. Put
\[
\alpha=\sqrt{\frac54}.
\]
For nonnegative integers \(n\) and \(z\), if
\[
4z^2\le 5n^2<4(z+1)^2,
\]
then
\[
z\le n\alpha<z+1.
\]
Indeed, all the quantities involved are nonnegative, so inequalities may be compared by squaring. Since \(\alpha^2=5/4\), the first integer inequality gives
\[
z^2\le \frac{5n^2}{4}=(n\alpha)^2,
\]
and hence \(z\le n\alpha\). The second gives
\[
(n\alpha)^2=\frac{5n^2}{4}<(z+1)^2,
\]
and hence \(n\alpha<z+1\). Thus \(z\le n\alpha<z+1\), which is precisely the assertion
\[
\left\lfloor n\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=z.
\]

We apply this criterion to the four sequence terms occurring in the recurrence at \(n=140\).

For \(n=161\), take \(z=180\). Direct integer arithmetic gives
\[
4\cdot 180^2=129600,
\qquad
5\cdot 161^2=129605,
\qquad
4\cdot 181^2=131044.
\]
Therefore
\[
4\cdot180^2\le 5\cdot161^2<4\cdot181^2,
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor161\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=180.
\]
Also \(\lfloor161/4\rfloor=40\). Consequently,
\[
a(161)=2\cdot161+180+40=322+180+40=542.
\]

For \(n=157\), take \(z=175\). We have
\[
4\cdot175^2=122500,
\qquad
5\cdot157^2=123245,
\qquad
4\cdot176^2=123904.
\]
Hence
\[
4\cdot175^2\le 5\cdot157^2<4\cdot176^2,
\]
and therefore
\[
\left\lfloor157\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=175.
\]
Since \(\lfloor157/4\rfloor=39\), it follows that
\[
a(157)=2\cdot157+175+39=314+175+39=528.
\]

For \(n=144\), take \(z=160\). The relevant integer values are
\[
4\cdot160^2=102400,
\qquad
5\cdot144^2=103680,
\qquad
4\cdot161^2=103684.
\]
Thus
\[
4\cdot160^2\le 5\cdot144^2<4\cdot161^2,
\]
which yields
\[
\left\lfloor144\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=160.
\]
Moreover, \(\lfloor144/4\rfloor=36\), so
\[
a(144)=2\cdot144+160+36=288+160+36=484.
\]

Finally, for \(n=140\), take \(z=156\). We calculate
\[
4\cdot156^2=97344,
\qquad
5\cdot140^2=98000,
\qquad
4\cdot157^2=98596.
\]
It follows that
\[
4\cdot156^2\le 5\cdot140^2<4\cdot157^2,
\]
so
\[
\left\lfloor140\sqrt{\frac54}\right\rfloor=156.
\]
Also \(\lfloor140/4\rfloor=35\). Hence
\[
a(140)=2\cdot140+156+35=280+156+35=471.
\]

The conjectured recurrence, specialized to \(n=140\), asserts
\[
a(140+21)=a(140+17)+a(140+4)-a(140),
\]
that is,
\[
a(161)=a(157)+a(144)-a(140).
\]
But the values just established give
\[
a(157)+a(144)-a(140)=528+484-471=541,
\]
whereas
\[
a(161)=542.
\]
Thus the two sides differ by \(1\). The recurrence fails at the admissible index \(n=140\), and therefore the claim that it holds for every \(n\ge1\) is false.
